---
title: "BFS Layers: Why the First Visit Is Shortest"
description: "Memorisable mathematical reasoning for algorithm interviews, with a worked example and proof."
---

## When to recognise this technique

When the question asks for minimum moves or minimum edges on an unweighted graph.

## Start with the question

**How can a queue certify the shortest path without checking all possible paths?**

## Formula worth memorising

$$
dist(v)=dist(u)+1\quad\text{for a first-discovered }v\in N(u)
$$

**Every symbol explained:** dist(u) is the already-known minimum number of edges from the start to u; N(u) is the set of neighbours; v is a newly discovered neighbour whose distance is one more.

**Substitute actual values:** If A connects to B and C, and B connects to D, BFS begins dist(A)=0, then dist(B)=dist(C)=1, then dist(D)=2. A path to D cannot use fewer than 2 edges because BFS already examined all vertices at depths 0 and 1.

## Why the mathematics works

A FIFO queue processes all distance-k vertices before distance-(k+1) vertices. The earliest discovery of a vertex must therefore use a shortest-edge-count path; marking on enqueue avoids duplicate discoveries.

## Limits and counterexamples

This proof assumes every edge has equal unit cost. Weighted graphs require other methods, such as Dijkstra for nonnegative weights or 0–1 BFS for weights 0 and 1.

## The 20-second memory card

**Memorise: The queue maintains distance layers; first discovery yields shortest number of edges.**

Try explaining the formula aloud using the numerical example, then reproduce the proof from memory. An interview answer must justify the relationship, not just quote it.

**Practice problems:** Word Ladder; Minimum Knight Moves.
